title: Another Georgia Officer Accused of Flock Misuse. The Safeguards Keep Failing After the Fact.
dek: A Houston County school resource officer has been suspended after an audit found alleged misuse of Flock license plate reader data, adding to a growing series of Georgia cases that expose a basic problem with surveillance safeguards: too often, they identify abuse only after someone has already been searched.
author: Ocmulgee Free Press Staff
featuredImageAlt: A Flock Safety automated license plate reader camera mounted beside a roadway.
featuredImageCaption: Flock Safety automated license plate reader camera.
body: Another Georgia law enforcement officer has been accused of misusing Flock Safety's automated license plate reader system, and once again the alleged misconduct was discovered only after the surveillance had already happened.

The Houston County Sheriff's Office says Deputy Sierra Carroll, a school resource officer, was suspended without pay on August 17 pending termination after an internal audit found that she had misused Flock Safety license plate reader data. Sheriff Matt Moulton said the matter was referred to the District Attorney's Office for possible criminal charges. As of the latest public reporting reviewed by The Ocmulgee Free Press, Carroll had not been criminally charged, and the investigation remained active.

Carroll was hired by the sheriff's office on April 28, 2025, and assigned to the School Resource Unit, according to the agency. The sheriff's office has not publicly disclosed what vehicles were allegedly searched, how many improper searches were identified, who may have been targeted or what prompted auditors to examine Carroll's activity.

Those unanswered questions matter because this is no longer an abstract debate about whether a surveillance system could be abused. Georgia now has a growing list of cases in which law enforcement personnel have been accused of doing exactly that.
## The pattern is getting harder to dismiss

One week before Carroll's suspension, three former Bibb County Sheriff's Office deputies were arrested after an audit found they allegedly used Flock license plate data for personal, non-law enforcement purposes involving people with whom they had personal relationships.

Joseph Marquee Callaway, Coznavian Stubbs and Toni Cierra Lewis were each charged with violation of oath by a public officer, misuse of license plate data and stalking-related offenses. Callaway also faced an additional charge involving the unauthorized request or disclosure of criminal history record information. Stubbs and Lewis resigned during the investigation, and Callaway resigned shortly after his arrest.

That Bibb County investigation reportedly began after Flock Safety notified the sheriff's office of possible irregularities. In other words, the system's audit trail did help expose the alleged conduct. It did not prevent the searches from occurring in the first place.

Just three days after the Bibb County arrests, former Milledgeville Police Major Brandon Sellers turned himself in after investigators said the Flock account assigned to him had been used for non-work-related purposes. Sellers was fired and charged with misdemeanor misuse of captured license plate data and felony violation of oath by a public officer. His case was referred for prosecution.

And the Middle Georgia cases followed an earlier investigation in Albany. In July, five Albany Police Department officers were arrested and fired after a Georgia Bureau of Investigation inquiry that began when an internal audit found officers had allegedly acquired and retained license plate data for non-law-enforcement purposes on multiple occasions.

Taken individually, each case involves separate people, separate agencies and allegations that must be proven in court. Taken together, they expose the same structural weakness: authorized access to a powerful surveillance database can be turned toward an unauthorized purpose before an audit, supervisor or automated system catches it.
## 'Accountability' after the search is not prevention

Sheriff Moulton has emphasized that Houston County has accountability measures in place and that Flock searches require specific case information. After the Albany arrests, he told WGXA that misuse of the system betrays public trust and said his agency was monitoring its own users more closely.

That makes the Carroll case especially significant. The alleged misuse was found inside an agency that had already been publicly discussing the exact risk, had already pointed to its safeguards and had already increased scrutiny because of misconduct elsewhere.
The audit apparently worked in one sense. It identified alleged misuse. But that should not be confused with a system that prevented misuse.
A digital audit trail is evidence of what happened. It is not a lock on the door.

If an officer with valid credentials can conduct an improper search and the system merely records the action for someone to discover later, then the protection depends on how quickly, how often and how seriously those logs are reviewed. An audit performed months later may establish accountability, but it cannot undo the surveillance of a person who should never have been searched.
That distinction has become impossible to ignore as more agencies announce misconduct only after retrospective audits.
## Flock itself is now changing the rules

Flock Safety's own response to recent abuse reports is revealing. In August, CEO Garrett Langley publicly apologized after reports of officers using license plate reader systems for personal surveillance. The company then announced that safeguards previously left optional would become mandatory across its law enforcement network.

Under the announced changes, vehicle searches must be tied to a specific criminal case and offense type. Flock also said it would expand automated auditing across all law enforcement customers to flag unusual searches. Reporting on the changes noted that the automated auditing feature had previously been enabled by only about one-third of agencies using the platform.

Flock also announced that its default vehicle-location data retention period would be reduced from 30 days to seven days, while allowing evidence connected to active investigations to be preserved longer through a new evidence mode.

Those changes are an acknowledgment of something privacy advocates have argued for years: access controls and written policies are not enough when the system allows a user to search a vast pool of vehicle-location information with a few keystrokes.

A requirement to enter a case number may improve accountability. Automated anomaly detection may catch suspicious patterns sooner. Shorter retention may reduce how much historical location data is available. None of those measures changes the central fact that the system still relies heavily on trusted users not abusing their access.
## The public should not have to wait for the next arrest

Law enforcement agencies routinely defend Flock by pointing to successful investigations, stolen vehicle recoveries, missing-person cases and the existence of search logs. Those are legitimate considerations. ALPR technology can be useful in legitimate police work.
But usefulness does not answer the oversight question.

The issue is not whether police can identify examples in which Flock helped solve a crime. The issue is whether agencies can prove that every search of a person's movements had a legitimate law enforcement purpose, whether improper searches can be stopped before they happen and whether the public receives enough information to independently evaluate those safeguards.
The recent Georgia cases suggest that the answer is not nearly as comforting as the sales pitch.

Albany had an audit. Bibb County had an audit. Milledgeville investigated an assigned account. Houston County had accountability measures and says it increased scrutiny after the Albany scandal. Yet officers in each of those jurisdictions were still accused of misusing plate reader data.
That does not prove every Flock search is improper. It proves that 'we have safeguards' is not the end of the conversation.
It should be the beginning of the audit.
## Questions Houston County still needs to answer

The public deserves more than confirmation that an employee was suspended. Houston County should disclose, consistent with applicable law, how many searches were determined to be improper, the time period involved, whether the same vehicle or person was searched repeatedly, whether any searches involved someone personally connected to the deputy, how the activity was discovered, how long it continued before detection and whether supervisors had previously reviewed the relevant audit logs.

The sheriff's office should also explain how frequently Flock searches are audited, what patterns trigger review, whether supervisors independently verify case numbers against actual incident records and what changes will be made following this investigation.
Those are not anti-police questions. They are basic oversight questions for any government agency operating a system capable of recording and searching the movements of ordinary people.

Flock Safety and law enforcement agencies have repeatedly asked the public to trust that the technology is used responsibly. The recent arrests, suspensions and policy changes across Georgia make a different standard more appropriate.
Do not ask the public to trust the safeguards. Show that they work.
And if the safeguard only activates after someone has already abused the system, stop calling it prevention.
